_comment: Who each quoted voice was, one short note per speaker, keyed by the exact `who` string of the quote registries (ui/emigration-quarter-bonuses.js QUARTER_QUOTES, ui/emigration-displaced-quotes.js). Read by scripts/gen-pedia-voices.mjs, which refuses to run when a registry speaker has no note here, so adding a quote means adding its speaker. Plain statements of role, place and time only; the quote's own source line already names the work. Every note is English-only by design, like the quotes themselves.
Abu Firas al-Hamdani: Abu Firas al-Hamdani (932 to 968) was a Hamdanid prince and Arabic poet of Aleppo. Captured by the Byzantines, he wrote his best-known poems, the Rumiyyat, during years of captivity in Constantinople.
Abu Tammam (attr.): Abu Tammam (about 796 to 845) was an Arabic poet born near Damascus who worked in Egypt before finding patrons at the Abbasid court in Baghdad. He also compiled the Hamasa, an influential anthology of early Arabic verse. The couplet is grouped with his verses by al-Jahiz; other early sources quote it without a name.
Adam Mickiewicz: Adam Mickiewicz (1798 to 1855) is the national poet of Poland. Exiled from the Russian partition, he wrote his epic Pan Tadeusz in Paris after the failed uprising of 1830 to 1831, and never saw his homeland again.
Adam Smith: Adam Smith (1723 to 1790) was a Scottish moral philosopher and the founding figure of modern economics. The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, describes how exchange and the division of labor create a commercial society.
Aelius Aristides: Aelius Aristides (117 to about 181) was a Greek orator from Mysia. His Roman Oration, delivered in the capital, praises the empire as a single marketplace fed by every land and sea.
Aeneas, in Virgil: Aeneas is the Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid (19 BCE), the founding epic of Rome. He escapes the sack of Troy carrying his father and leads the survivors across the sea in search of a new home in Italy.
Ahmad Baba al-Timbukti: Ahmad Baba (1556 to 1627) was the most celebrated scholar of Timbuktu. After the Moroccan conquest of Songhai in 1591 he was deported in chains to Marrakesh, where he wrote of his longing for home; he was allowed to return only in 1608.
Aksumite coinage: The kingdom of Aksum, in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, struck its own gold, silver and bronze coins from the third century onward. Their short Greek and Ge'ez legends are among the few Aksumite words to survive in the kingdom's own voice.
Alan Qo'a, in the Secret History of the: Alan Qo'a is the legendary ancestress of the Mongol ruling clan in the Secret History of the Mongols, written in the thirteenth century. She teaches her sons unity with a bundle of arrow-shafts that cannot be broken together.
Alexander Pushkin: Alexander Pushkin (1799 to 1837) is Russia's national poet. The Bronze Horseman, his narrative poem of 1833, opens with Peter the Great resolving to found St Petersburg on the Neva marshes.
Alexandre Exquemelin: Alexandre Exquemelin (about 1645 to 1707) sailed to Tortuga as an indentured servant of the French West India Company, was sold twice, and after gaining his freedom joined the buccaneers as a surgeon. His Buccaneers of America (1678) is the classic eyewitness account of the pirates of the Caribbean.
Ali-Akbar Dehkhoda: Ali-Akbar Dehkhoda (1879 to 1956) was an Iranian journalist, satirist and lexicographer of the Constitutional Revolution. He fled to Europe after the coup of 1908 and later compiled the great Dehkhoda Dictionary of Persian.
Apion, an Egyptian in the Roman fleet: Apion was a young man from a village in the Fayum who enlisted in the Roman fleet in the second century. His letter home from Misenum, preserved on papyrus, tells his father he arrived safely, took a Roman name, and sends his portrait.
Appian: Appian of Alexandria (about 95 to 165) was a Greek historian of Rome. His account of the Punic Wars describes the harbors of Carthage in the city's final years.
Articles of Bartholomew Roberts's crew: Pirate crews of the early eighteenth century agreed written articles before a voyage. Those of Bartholomew Roberts's crew, printed in A General History of the Pyrates (1724), gave every man a vote and an equal share of provisions.
Ashoka: Ashoka (reigned about 268 to 232 BCE) was the third Mauryan emperor. After the bloody conquest of Kalinga he embraced Buddhism and had his edicts carved on rocks and pillars across India, the earliest surviving royal inscriptions of the subcontinent.
Ashurbanipal: Ashurbanipal (reigned 669 to about 631 BCE) was the last great king of Assyria. He boasted of his scribal training and assembled at Nineveh the library of cuneiform tablets that preserved much of Mesopotamian literature.
Babur: Babur (1483 to 1530) was a Timurid prince of Fergana who lost his homeland as a youth, wandered the mountains of Central Asia, took Kabul, and in 1526 founded the Mughal Empire in India. His memoir, the Baburnama, is one of the great autobiographies of the age.
Bartholomew Roberts: Bartholomew Roberts (1682 to 1722), called Black Bart, was a Welsh sailor who became the most successful pirate captain of the Golden Age, taking hundreds of ships before he was killed in action off West Africa.
Bayeux Tapestry: The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidered narrative nearly seventy meters long, made in the 1070s, that tells the story of the Norman conquest of England. Its Latin captions, or tituli, run above the scenes.
Benito Juárez: Benito Juárez (1806 to 1872), a Zapotec from Oaxaca, was president of Mexico through the Reform War and the French intervention. His manifesto on returning to the capital in 1867 gave Mexico one of its best-known maxims.
Calvin Coolidge: Calvin Coolidge (1872 to 1933) was the thirtieth president of the United States. The line comes from his 1925 address to newspaper editors, a speech that goes on to say that Americans idealize far more than wealth.
Canadian Boat-Song: The Canadian Boat-Song appeared anonymously in Blackwood's Magazine in 1829, presented as a Gaelic song of Highland emigrants rowing on the St Lawrence. Its authorship has never been settled.
Cao Xueqin: Cao Xueqin (about 1715 to 1763) wrote Dream of the Red Chamber, the greatest novel of the Qing dynasty, a portrait of an aristocratic household in decline. The line is a couplet hung in a study within the novel.
Carl von Clausewitz: Carl von Clausewitz (1780 to 1831) was a Prussian general and director of the war academy in Berlin. His unfinished treatise On War, published after his death, remains the most influential work of military theory in the West.
Cem Sultan: Cem Sultan (1459 to 1495) was an Ottoman prince who lost the succession war to his brother Bayezid II and fled abroad. He spent the rest of his life as a captive guest of the Knights of Rhodes, the French crown and the Pope, and wrote poetry in exile.
Chao Cuo: Chao Cuo (died 154 BCE) was a statesman of the early Han dynasty. His memorials to the throne argued for settling farmers on the northern frontier and for making the first settlers comfortable enough that others would follow.
Chekilli, Creek head chief: Chekilli was head chief of the Lower Creek towns. In 1735 he recited the Kasihta migration legend to the colonial governor at Savannah, an account of how his people's ancestors came from the west and settled on either side of the river.
Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce: Chief Joseph (about 1840 to 1904) led a band of the Nez Perce through a fighting retreat of over a thousand miles in 1877 before surrendering. Exiled with his people to Indian Territory, he argued in Washington and in print for their return.
Choe Chiwon: Choe Chiwon (857 to after 908) was sent from Silla to Tang China at the age of twelve, passed the imperial examination there, and served the Tang before returning home. He is remembered as the founding figure of Korean literature in Chinese.
Cyrus the Younger: Cyrus the Younger (died 401 BCE) was an Achaemenid prince and satrap of Lydia. In Xenophon's Oeconomicus he shows a Spartan visitor the garden at Sardis and says he planted some of the trees himself.
Dante Alighieri: Dante Alighieri (1265 to 1321) wrote the Divine Comedy in exile, having been banished from Florence in 1302 under sentence of death. In the Paradiso his ancestor Cacciaguida foretells to him how bitter the bread of others will taste.
Denis Diderot: Denis Diderot (1713 to 1784) was a French philosopher and the chief editor of the Encyclopédie, the great work of the Enlightenment. The line comes from his own article defining the project.
Dido, in Virgil: Dido, in Virgil's Aeneid, is the queen who fled Tyre after her brother murdered her husband and founded Carthage on the African coast. When the shipwrecked Trojans reach her city she welcomes them as one refugee to another.
Diviciacus the Aeduan: Diviciacus was a druid and leader of the Aedui, a Gaulish people allied to Rome. Caesar records his plea, made in 58 BCE, that the Gauls would have to emigrate en masse if the Germans under Ariovistus were not stopped.
Diwan-i-Khas inscription, Red Fort: The Diwan-i-Khas is the hall of private audience in the Red Fort at Delhi, completed under Shah Jahan around 1648. The Persian couplet is inscribed on its walls; it is often credited to Amir Khusrow, but does not appear in his surviving works.
Du Fu: Du Fu (712 to 770) is, with Li Bai, the most revered poet of the Tang dynasty. The An Lushan rebellion of 755 uprooted him and his family for the rest of his life, and displacement and separation run through his poems.
El Deportado: El Deportado is a Mexican corrido, a narrative ballad, recorded in the 1920s. It tells of a man who leaves Mexico during the Revolution for work in the United States and is later deported.
Emperor Armah: Armah was a king of Aksum in the early seventh century, remembered in Islamic tradition as the Negus who gave refuge to the first Muslims fleeing Mecca. His coins carry a Ge'ez legend wishing the people gladness.
Emperor Wen of Han: Emperor Wen (reigned 180 to 157 BCE) was the fifth emperor of the Han dynasty, remembered for frugal rule, light taxes and personal attention to farming. The line opens one of his edicts preserved in the Book of Han.
Ferdinand Freiligrath: Ferdinand Freiligrath (1810 to 1876) was a German poet who watched emigrants boarding Rhine boats for America and wrote The Emigrants in 1832. He later went into exile himself for his political verse.
François Bernier: François Bernier (1620 to 1688) was a French physician who spent twelve years in India at the Mughal court. His Travels in the Mogul Empire describe the wealth that flowed into Hindustan and stayed there.
Frederick Douglass: Frederick Douglass (about 1818 to 1895) escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the leading African American abolitionist, orator and writer of his century. My Bondage and My Freedom is the second of his three autobiographies.
Frederick II: Frederick II of Prussia (reigned 1740 to 1786), called the Great, wrote the words in the margin of a petition in the first year of his reign, ruling that Catholic schools could stay open. The note became the emblem of Prussian religious toleration.
Frontinus: Sextus Julius Frontinus (about 40 to 103) was a Roman senator and water commissioner of the city of Rome. His treatise On the Aqueducts sets the useful engineering of Rome above the idle monuments of Egypt and Greece.
Fukuzawa Yukichi: Fukuzawa Yukichi (1835 to 1901) was the foremost educator and reformer of Meiji Japan and the founder of Keio University. An Encouragement of Learning, begun in 1872, sold in the millions.
Ganda proverb: The Baganda of the Buganda kingdom, on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, have a rich tradition of Luganda proverbs. This one was collected in Ferdinand Walser's anthology Luganda Proverbs.
Garcilaso de la Vega: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega (1539 to 1616) was born in Cuzco to a Spanish conquistador and an Inca princess. He left Peru for Spain in 1560 and there wrote the Royal Commentaries of the Incas, the first great history of the Andes by a writer of Inca descent.
George W. Harkins, Choctaw chief: George W. Harkins (1810 to 1890) was a district chief of the Choctaw. His Farewell Letter to the American People, published in 1832 as the Choctaw were removed west of the Mississippi, is one of the earliest protests against Indian removal in the removed people's own words.
Guanzi: The Guanzi is a Chinese compendium of political and economic thought attributed to Guan Zhong, minister of the state of Qi in the seventh century BCE. Sima Qian quotes its maxim on granaries and propriety in his Records of the Grand Historian.
Guðmundur Stefánsson: Guðmundur Stefánsson was an Icelandic farmer who emigrated to Wisconsin in 1873 with his family, among the first Icelanders to settle in North America. His letters home describe the departure and the welcome. His son became the poet Stephan G. Stephansson.
Hafez: Hafez (about 1325 to 1390) of Shiraz is the most beloved lyric poet of Persian. His Divan of ghazals is still used in Iran for divination and recited from memory.
Ham Mukasa: Ham Mukasa (about 1868 to 1956) was a Buganda chief and writer. He accompanied the Katikkiro, the kingdom's prime minister, to the coronation of Edward VII in 1902 and published an account of the journey.
Hamlin Garland, of his mother: Hamlin Garland (1860 to 1940) grew up on a succession of farms as his family moved west across Wisconsin, Iowa and Dakota. A Son of the Middle Border recalls his mother's grief at each uprooting.
Hammurabi: Hammurabi (reigned about 1792 to 1750 BCE) was the king of Babylon who unified Mesopotamia and had his laws carved on a stele. Its prologue names his purpose: that the strong might not oppress the weak.
He Zhizhang: He Zhizhang (659 to 744) was a Tang poet and official who spent nearly fifty years in the capital before retiring to his native Zhejiang. His poem on returning home is among the best known in Chinese.
Heinrich Heine: Heinrich Heine (1797 to 1856) was a German poet born in Düsseldorf. He moved to Paris in 1831 and lived there in exile for the rest of his life, his works banned in Prussia.
Henry M. Brackenridge, at Cahokia: Henry Marie Brackenridge (1786 to 1871) was an American lawyer and writer who visited the great mounds at Cahokia in 1811 and was among the first to describe them in print.
Henry ʻŌpūkahaʻia: Henry ʻŌpūkahaʻia (about 1792 to 1818) was orphaned in the wars of Hawaiian unification and sailed to New England as a youth in 1809. He died in Connecticut before he could return; his memoirs inspired the first missionaries to Hawaiʻi.
Herodotus: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (about 484 to 425 BCE) wrote the Histories, the first great work of history in the Greek tradition. He traveled widely and described Egypt, Babylon and Persia as a curious outsider.
Herodotus (after Hecataeus): Herodotus of Halicarnassus (about 484 to 425 BCE) wrote the Histories, the first great work of history in the Greek tradition. The description of Egypt as the gift of the river is one he took over from the earlier geographer Hecataeus of Miletus.
Herodotus, on the Phocaeans: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (about 484 to 425 BCE) wrote the Histories, the first great work of history in the Greek tradition. He tells how the Phocaeans of Ionia abandoned their city to the Persians around 540 BCE, and how more than half of them turned back for love of it.
Hesiod, of his father: Hesiod (about 700 BCE) was a Boeotian farmer-poet, author of Works and Days and the Theogony. He tells how his father left Aeolian Cyme in Asia Minor to escape poverty and settled at Ascra near Mount Helicon.
Homeric Epigram IV: The Homeric Epigrams are short poems attached to the ancient Life of Homer and attributed to the poet. This one voices a wandering singer resolving to leave Cyme for another country.
Hristo Botev: Hristo Botev (1848 to 1876) was a Bulgarian revolutionary and poet who lived as an émigré in Romania. He died leading a band of insurgents across the Danube during the April Uprising against Ottoman rule.
Hávamál: The Hávamál, the Sayings of the High One, is a poem of the Poetic Edda preserved in the thirteenth-century Codex Regius of Iceland. Its gnomic verses put practical wisdom in the mouth of Odin.
Hồ Nguyên Trừng: Hồ Nguyên Trừng (1374 to 1446) was the eldest son of the Vietnamese emperor Hồ Quý Ly. Taken to China after the Ming conquest of 1407, he served the Ming as an artillery engineer and wrote a memoir of the people of his lost homeland.
Iio Tsunefusa: Iio Tsunefusa was a poet and official of the Ashikaga shogunate in the fifteenth century. His verse on the capital laid waste by the Ōnin War (1467 to 1477) became the epitaph of the old Kyoto.
Inca Garcilaso de la Vega: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega (1539 to 1616) was born in Cuzco to a Spanish conquistador and an Inca princess. He left Peru for Spain in 1560 and there wrote the Royal Commentaries of the Incas, the first great history of the Andes by a writer of Inca descent.
Isaac Adams, of Urmia: Isaac Adams was an Assyrian Christian from near Urmia, in north-western Iran, who emigrated to the United States in 1889 with almost nothing. He trained as a physician and wrote Persia by a Persian about his homeland and his journey.
Ishikawa Takuboku: Ishikawa Takuboku (1886 to 1912) was a Japanese poet who left his village in Iwate for Hokkaido and then Tokyo, living in poverty. A Handful of Sand, his collection of three-line tanka, made him famous shortly before he died of tuberculosis at twenty-six.
Ivan Bunin: Ivan Bunin (1870 to 1953) fled Bolshevik Russia in 1920 and lived in exile in France. In 1933 he became the first Russian writer awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Ivan Vazov: Ivan Vazov (1850 to 1921) is called the patriarch of Bulgarian literature. His poem The Bulgarian Language defends the mother tongue of a people newly freed from Ottoman rule.
Jacob A. Riis: Jacob Riis (1849 to 1914) emigrated from Denmark to New York in 1870 as a penniless carpenter. He became a police reporter and photographer whose How the Other Half Lives exposed the tenements; The Making of an American is his memoir.
Jeong Yak-yong, on reaching his place of: Jeong Yak-yong (1762 to 1836), pen name Dasan, was the greatest scholar of late Joseon. Banished in 1801 in a purge of Catholics and reformers, he spent eighteen years in exile at Gangjin and wrote most of his works there.
Joachim du Bellay: Joachim du Bellay (about 1522 to 1560) was a poet of the French Pléiade. The Regrets, sonnets written during four years in the service of a cardinal in Rome, are the classic French poems of homesickness.
John Roscoe: John Roscoe (1861 to 1932) was an English missionary and anthropologist who lived in Buganda for twenty-five years. The Baganda (1911) is his ethnography of the kingdom's customs and economy.
John Stedman, labourer, from Upper Canad: John Stedman was a farm labourer from Surrey who emigrated to Upper Canada in 1832 with assistance from his parish. His letter home was printed to encourage others to follow.
Josiah Henson: Josiah Henson (1789 to 1883) escaped slavery in Kentucky in 1830 and reached Upper Canada, where he founded a settlement for other fugitives. His autobiography is often said to have inspired Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom.
José Martí: José Martí (1853 to 1895) was the poet and apostle of Cuban independence. Deported from Cuba as a teenager, he lived most of his adult life in exile, chiefly in New York, and died in the first weeks of the war he had organized.
Julius Caesar: Julius Caesar (100 to 44 BCE) conquered Gaul between 58 and 50 BCE and wrote his own account of the campaigns, the Commentaries on the Gallic War. It remains the principal written source on the Gauls, from their conqueror's hand.
Kahlil Gibran: Kahlil Gibran (1883 to 1931) emigrated from Bsharri in Lebanon to Boston as a boy in 1895. He wrote in Arabic and English, and his book The Prophet is among the most translated works of the twentieth century.
Kauṭilya: Kauṭilya, also called Chanakya, is the author to whom the Arthaśāstra, the Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, is traditionally ascribed. Tradition makes him the minister who raised Chandragupta Maurya to the throne; the received text dates from later centuries.
Khan Omurtag: Omurtag (reigned 814 to 831) was khan of the Bulgars. His building inscriptions, carved in Greek, record his palaces and bridges and reflect on the mortality of the builder.
King George Tupou I: George Tupou I (about 1797 to 1893) united the Tongan islands and, in 1875, granted a written constitution that abolished serfdom and declared every person in the kingdom free. Tonga remained the one Pacific kingdom never colonized.
King Sejong: Sejong (reigned 1418 to 1450) was the fourth king of Joseon Korea. In 1443 he created Hangul, the Korean alphabet, and explained in its preface that the speech of Korea differed from that of China and needed its own letters.
Kovur Kizhar: Kovur Kizhar was a Tamil poet of the Sangam age whose poems are preserved in the Purananuru anthology. Here he pleads with a Chola king for the life of a rival's traveling poet.
Le Page du Pratz, among the Natchez: Antoine-Simon Le Page du Pratz (about 1695 to 1775) lived for sixteen years in French Louisiana, eight of them beside the Natchez, a mound-building people of the lower Mississippi. His History of Louisiana is a principal source on them.
Lee Chew: Lee Chew left a farming village near Canton for San Francisco in the 1870s and became a laundryman and merchant in New York. His life story was published in The Independent in 1903.
Leo Africanus: Leo Africanus (about 1494 to about 1554), born al-Hasan al-Wazzan in Granada and raised in Fez, traveled to Timbuktu and across the Sahara as a young diplomat. Captured by pirates and baptised in Rome, he wrote his Description of Africa in Italian.
Liliʻuokalani: Liliʻuokalani (1838 to 1917) was the last queen of Hawaiʻi. Deposed in 1893 by a group backed by American forces, she wrote Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen in 1898 to plead her people's case against annexation.
Livy, on King Ambigatus sending out the: Livy (59 BCE to 17 CE) wrote the history of Rome from its foundation. In his fifth book he tells the story of the Gaulish king Ambigatus, who sent his nephews out with surplus population to find new lands, and so began the Gallic migrations into Italy.
Ma Huan: Ma Huan (about 1380 to 1460) was a Muslim interpreter who sailed on three of Zheng He's expeditions. His Overall Survey of the Ocean's Shores (1433) describes the ports of Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean.
Magna Carta: Magna Carta, the Great Charter, was sealed by King John of England at Runnymede in 1215 under pressure from his barons. Clause 39, on lawful judgment, became the foundation of the English idea of liberty under law.
Marco Polo: Marco Polo (1254 to 1324) was a Venetian merchant who spent some seventeen years in the service of Kublai Khan. His Travels, dictated in a Genoese prison, describe the Mongol post-road system across Asia.
Mary Antin: Mary Antin (1881 to 1949) emigrated from Polotsk in the Russian Empire to Boston in 1894 at the age of thirteen. The Promised Land, her memoir of leaving the Pale and becoming American, was a bestseller in 1912.
Miguel de Cervantes: Miguel de Cervantes (1547 to 1616) wrote Don Quixote, the first modern novel. He had himself been a soldier, a captive in Algiers for five years, and a tax collector before he wrote it.
Mikhail Lermontov: Mikhail Lermontov (1814 to 1841) was the leading Russian poet of the generation after Pushkin. He wrote Clouds in 1840 on the day he left St Petersburg for his second exile to the Caucasus, where he was killed in a duel the next year.
Mom Rajothai: Mom Rajothai (1819 to 1867) was a Siamese nobleman who served as interpreter to the embassy King Mongkut sent to Queen Victoria in 1857. His Nirat London is the first Thai travel poem about Europe.
Montesquieu: Montesquieu (1689 to 1755) was a French political philosopher. The Spirit of the Laws (1748), his study of governments and their customs, argued that commerce softens manners and links peoples.
Mpu Prapanca: Mpu Prapanca was a Buddhist court poet of Majapahit in Java. His Nagarakretagama, completed in 1365, praises King Hayam Wuruk and describes the kingdom and the foreigners drawn to it.
Muna, to her husband bound for Lhasa: Muna is the wife in Muna Madan (1936), the most beloved poem in Nepali, by Laxmi Prasad Devkota. Her husband Madan leaves for Lhasa to trade, and she pleads that a contented heart is worth more than gold.
Murasaki Shikibu: Murasaki Shikibu (about 973 to about 1014) was a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court and the author of The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel. The passage describes the crowds at the Kamo festival in the capital.
Nasir Khusraw: Nasir Khusraw (1004 to after 1070) was a Persian poet, philosopher and Ismaili missionary. Driven from Balkh for his faith, he spent his last decades in the remote valley of Yumgan in Badakhshan, writing of his exile.
Nedîm: Nedîm (about 1681 to 1730) was the court poet of the Ottoman Tulip Era under Ahmed III. His songs celebrate the pleasure gardens of Sa'dabad on the Golden Horn; he died during the revolt that ended the era.
Nguyễn Trãi: Nguyễn Trãi (1380 to 1442) was a Vietnamese scholar and strategist who helped Lê Lợi drive out the Ming occupation. He lived through the years of foreign rule and returned to his family's home at Côn Sơn after the war.
Ningal, queen of Ur, mourning her people: Ningal is the goddess of the city of Ur in Sumerian religion. In the Lament for Ur, composed after the city's fall around 2000 BCE, she weeps for her scattered people, a form of city lament that Babylon inherited.
Njáll Þorgeirsson: Njáll Þorgeirsson is the wise lawyer at the center of Njáls saga, the greatest of the Icelandic sagas, set around the year 1000. His saying on law and land is the best-known sentence in Icelandic.
Oda Nobunaga: Oda Nobunaga (1534 to 1582) was the first of the three unifiers of Japan. At Gifu in 1568 he issued an edict for free markets and open guilds, breaking the monopolies of the old trade associations.
Omar Khayyám: Omar Khayyám (1048 to 1131) was a Persian mathematician and astronomer of Nishapur to whom a great body of quatrains, the Rubáiyát, is attributed. This one prizes a loaf of bread and a quiet corner above a sultan's estate.
Ono no Takamura: Ono no Takamura (802 to 853) was a Heian scholar and poet banished to the Oki Islands in 838 for refusing to sail on an embassy to China. His poem of departure is in the Kokin Wakashū and the Hundred Poets anthology.
Orderic Vitalis: Orderic Vitalis (1075 to about 1142) was born in Shropshire to a Norman father and an English mother and sent at the age of ten to the abbey of Saint-Évroul in Normandy. His Ecclesiastical History is the fullest chronicle of the Norman world.
Orderic Vitalis, on the exiled William C: Orderic Vitalis (1075 to about 1142) was a monk of Saint-Évroul in Normandy and the chronicler of the Norman world. He describes William Clito, son of the imprisoned Duke Robert, carried into exile in France as a small boy and raised among strangers.
Ovid: Ovid (43 BCE to 17 CE) was the Roman poet of the Metamorphoses. In 8 CE Augustus banished him to Tomis on the Black Sea, and the Tristia, his poems of sorrow, describe his last night in Rome and his life among strangers.
Pedro Cieza de León: Pedro Cieza de León (about 1520 to 1554) was a Spanish soldier who traveled the length of the Andes in the 1540s and recorded what he saw of the Inca realm. His chronicles are among the most reliable early accounts of it.
Pericles: Pericles (about 495 to 429 BCE) was the leading statesman of democratic Athens. Thucydides gives him the Funeral Oration, in which he describes the character of the Athenians.
Periplus of Hanno: The Periplus of Hanno is a short Greek text recording a Carthaginian voyage of colonization down the Atlantic coast of Africa, traditionally dated to the fifth century BCE. It says it was inscribed in the temple of Baal at Carthage.
Popol Vuh: The Popol Vuh is the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya of highland Guatemala, written down in the sixteenth century from older tradition. It tells of the creation of people from maize and the migrations of the K'iche' ancestors.
Prince Myshkin, as Ippolit reports: Prince Myshkin is the guileless hero of Dostoevsky's novel The Idiot (1869). The saying that beauty will save the world is attributed to him by another character, Ippolit, and is never spoken in the author's own voice.
Prithvi Narayan Shah: Prithvi Narayan Shah (1723 to 1775), king of Gorkha, unified the kingdom of Nepal. His Divya Upadesh, the divine counsel dictated near the end of his life, describes Nepal as a yam between two stones, India and China.
Ramkhamhaeng Inscription: The Ramkhamhaeng Inscription, dated 1292, is the earliest known text in the Thai script. Attributed to King Ramkhamhaeng of Sukhothai, it describes a prosperous, free and festive kingdom.
Ricote the Morisco, in Cervantes: Ricote is a Morisco villager in the second part of Don Quixote (1615), expelled from Spain with the rest of his people between 1609 and 1614. Cervantes has him return in disguise and speak of his longing for the country that cast him out.
Robert P. Ashe: Robert Pickering Ashe (1857 to 1944) was an Anglican missionary in Buganda in the 1880s. His Chronicles of Uganda records the persecution of the first Christian converts and their flight to neighboring Ankole.
Rosalía de Castro: Rosalía de Castro (1837 to 1885) was the poet of Galicia, writing in Galician at a time when its people were emigrating in huge numbers to Cuba and Argentina. Her Cantares gallegos gave the emigrants their farewell song.
Saadi: Saadi of Shiraz (about 1210 to about 1291) is one of the most quoted poets of Persian. He left his city as the Mongols advanced and spent some thirty years traveling before returning to write the Bustan and the Gulistan.
Samguk Yusa: The Samguk Yusa, the Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms, was compiled by the Buddhist monk Iryeon in the thirteenth century. It preserves the legends and traditions of early Korea, including a picture of Silla's capital at its height.
Sei Shōnagon: Sei Shōnagon (about 966 to about 1025) was a lady-in-waiting to Empress Teishi at the Heian court. Her Pillow Book, a collection of observations and lists, opens with the seasons and their finest hours.
Seneca: Seneca the Younger (about 4 BCE to 65 CE) was a Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman. Banished to Corsica in 41 CE, he wrote his mother a consolation arguing that exile is bearable and that Rome itself is a city of newcomers.
Sennacherib: Sennacherib (reigned 705 to 681 BCE) was king of Assyria. He made Nineveh his capital and rebuilt it with new walls, palaces and canals, recording the work in inscriptions on its wall-slabs.
Shen Fu: Shen Fu (1763 to after 1809) was a minor Qing official and painter of Suzhou. His Six Records of a Floating Life is a tender memoir of his marriage and of a childhood spent looking closely at small things.
Sinuhe: Sinuhe is the narrator of the Story of Sinuhe, an Egyptian tale of the Middle Kingdom (about 1900 BCE). A courtier who flees Egypt on the death of the king, he prospers in Syria but longs to return home to be buried.
Socrates: Socrates (about 470 to 399 BCE) was the Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing himself. The line comes from the Apology, Plato's account of his speech at the trial that condemned him to death.
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (1648 to 1695) was a nun, poet and scholar of New Spain, the foremost writer of colonial Mexico. Her Reply to Sor Filotea defends a woman's right to study.
Stephan G. Stephansson: Stephan G. Stephansson (1853 to 1927) emigrated from Iceland to North America in 1873 and farmed in Wisconsin, North Dakota and finally Alberta. He is regarded as the greatest Icelandic poet of his time, though he never returned to live there.
Sugawara no Michizane: Sugawara no Michizane (845 to 903) was a scholar and minister of the Heian court. Exiled to Dazaifu in Kyushu in 901 through the intrigues of the Fujiwara, he died there; he was later deified as Tenjin, the patron of learning.
Süleyman the Magnificent (Muhibbî): Süleyman I (reigned 1520 to 1566), called the Magnificent, brought the Ottoman Empire to its height. Under the pen name Muhibbî he was also a prolific poet; this couplet is his best-known.
Takeda Shingen: Takeda Shingen (1521 to 1573) was one of the great warlords of Japan's Warring States period. His war banner bore four characters from Sun Tzu, wind, forest, fire and mountain.
Tecumseh: Tecumseh (1768 to 1813) was a Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of nations to resist the sale of their lands. His speeches survive only in the reports of others; he was killed at the Battle of the Thames in 1813.
Teresa of Ávila: Teresa of Ávila (1515 to 1582) was a Spanish Carmelite nun, mystic and reformer, and one of the great prose writers of the Spanish language. The short prayer was found written in her breviary.
The Tales of Ise: The Tales of Ise is a tenth-century Japanese collection of poems set in short prose episodes, following a nameless courtier usually identified with Ariwara no Narihira. Several episodes follow his journey away from the capital to the east.
Thucydides: Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BCE) was an Athenian general and the historian of the Peloponnesian War. Exiled for twenty years after failing to save Amphipolis, he used the time to research both sides of the war.
Thân Nhân Trung: Thân Nhân Trung (1419 to 1499) was a scholar-official of the Lê dynasty of Dai Viet. He composed the inscription for the first of the doctors' stelae at the Temple of Literature in Hanoi, which records the examination graduates of 1442.
Tiruvalluvar: Tiruvalluvar was the Tamil poet of the Tirukkural, a collection of 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love, composed sometime in the first centuries of the common era. It is the most revered work of Tamil literature.
Toghon Temür (attr.): Toghon Temür (1320 to 1370) was the last Yuan emperor of China. In 1368 he fled his capital Daidu, now Beijing, before the armies of the Ming; a lament for the lost city is attributed to him in later Mongol chronicles.
Tongan paddling song: William Mariner, an English youth held for four years in Tonga from 1806, later dictated an account of the islands that included this paddling song, sung by crews leaving the island of Vavaʻu.
Trần Hưng Đạo: Trần Hưng Đạo (about 1228 to 1300) was the general who defeated three Mongol invasions of Dai Viet. His Proclamation to the Officers, written before the invasion of 1285, called his commanders to discipline and training.
Victor Hugo: Victor Hugo (1802 to 1885) was the foremost French writer of the nineteenth century. He went into exile after the coup of 1851, lived nineteen years in the Channel Islands, and wrote his essay What Exile Is on Guernsey.
Walt Whitman: Walt Whitman (1819 to 1892) was the poet of Leaves of Grass. I Hear America Singing, added in 1860, is his catalogue of working people, each singing at their trade.
Wang Can: Wang Can (177 to 217) was a poet of the late Han who fled the fall of Chang'an and lived for years as a refugee in Jingzhou. His Rhapsody on Climbing the Tower is the classic Chinese poem of the exile's longing for home.
Wang Geon (Taejo): Wang Geon (877 to 943), posthumously Taejo, founded the Goryeo dynasty that gave Korea its name. His Ten Injunctions, left to his successors, survive in the official history of the dynasty.
Wang Yangming: Wang Yangming (1472 to 1529) was a Ming philosopher, general and official. His teaching of the unity of knowledge and action shaped Neo-Confucian thought in China, Korea and Japan.
Wayweleapy, Shawnee speaker: Wayweleapy was the principal speaker for the Shawnee chiefs of Wapakoneta, Ohio, at the council of 1832 at which the United States pressed them to remove west of the Mississippi. His words were recorded by the council's clerks.
William Blake: William Blake (1757 to 1827) was an English poet, painter and engraver. The verses from the preface to his poem Milton, later set to music as the hymn Jerusalem, contrast England's green land with its new mills.
William Bradford: William Bradford (1590 to 1657) was an English Separatist who fled to the Netherlands to escape persecution and sailed on the Mayflower in 1620. He governed Plymouth Colony for thirty years and wrote its history.
William Kirkpatrick: William Kirkpatrick (1754 to 1812) was an officer of the East India Company who led a mission to Kathmandu in 1793, the first British visit to Nepal. His Account of the Kingdom of Nepaul describes its terraced hills.
William Shakespeare: William Shakespeare (1564 to 1616) wrote Richard II around 1595. The lines belong to the dying John of Gaunt, who praises England before lamenting what its king has made of it.
Xu Jing: Xu Jing (1091 to 1153) was a member of the Song embassy to Goryeo in 1123. His Illustrated Account of Goryeo describes the kingdom's court and crafts, including the celadon the Koreans called kingfisher-colored.
Yi I (Yulgok): Yi I (1536 to 1584), pen name Yulgok, was one of the two great Confucian philosophers of Joseon Korea. His Essentials for Dispelling Ignorance (1577) was a primer for beginning students.
Yi Je-hyeon: Yi Je-hyeon (1287 to 1367) was a Goryeo scholar and statesman who spent long years in Yuan China attending the Goryeo kings held at the Mongol court. He wrote the poem on a mission far from home.
Yi Kyu-bo: Yi Kyu-bo (1168 to 1241) was the leading poet of Goryeo. He wrote this poem on Ganghwa Island, where the court had fled from the Mongol invasion, looking back toward the abandoned capital.
Yu Seong-ryong, on the flight from Seoul: Yu Seong-ryong (1542 to 1607) was chief state councillor of Joseon during the Japanese invasion of 1592. His Jingbirok, the Book of Corrections, records the court's flight from Seoul and the words of the people left behind.
Yuan Kai: Yuan Kai was a poet and official of the early Ming dynasty from Songjiang, near modern Shanghai, who served in the capital at Nanjing in the 1370s. He is remembered for a single much-anthologised poem on a letter from home.
Zheng He: Zheng He (1371 to 1433) was the Ming admiral who led seven great treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean. Before his last voyage he set up a stele at Changle recording how far the fleets had sailed.
Zhou Daguan: Zhou Daguan (about 1270 to 1350) was a Chinese envoy who lived at Angkor for a year in 1296 to 1297. His Customs of Cambodia is the only surviving eyewitness account of the Khmer Empire in its last great age.
a Chinese migrant from Taishan: Between 1910 and 1940 Chinese immigrants held at the Angel Island station in San Francisco Bay carved poems into the walls of the detention barracks. Most came from the Taishan district of Guangdong; the poets are anonymous.
a migrant writing from Chicago: During the Great Migration of 1916 to 1918, hundreds of thousands of African Americans left the rural South for northern cities. Letters they wrote home, collected by Emmett J. Scott, were published in the Journal of Negro History in 1919; the writers' names were withheld.
al-Kindi: Al-Kindi (about 801 to 873) was the first of the Arab philosophers, working in the House of Wisdom at Baghdad under the Abbasid caliphs. His treatise On First Philosophy urges the acceptance of truth from any source.
holehole bushi, a Hawaii plantation song: Holehole bushi are the work songs of Japanese immigrants on the sugar plantations of Hawaiʻi, named for the task of stripping cane leaves. Sung from the 1880s onward, they record the emigrants' hopes, hardships and settling down.
motto of the Kingdom of Tonga: The motto God and Tonga are my inheritance was adopted with the kingdom's coat of arms under George Tupou I in 1875 and remains on the national arms today.
the Charter Oath: The Charter Oath was proclaimed in the name of the Meiji Emperor in April 1868, at the start of the Meiji Restoration. Its five articles set the course of Japan's modernisation, the last promising to seek knowledge throughout the world.
the Inca nobles of Cuzco: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, born in Cuzco in 1539 to an Inca princess, grew up hearing his mother's kinsmen mourn the fall of their empire. He recorded their words in his Royal Commentaries of the Incas, written in Spain.
the Kaqchikel ancestors: The Annals of the Kaqchikels, written in the sixteenth century, record the traditions of the Kaqchikel Maya of highland Guatemala, including their ancestors' long migration from the legendary city of Tulan.
the Obsidian Stone, to the Kaqchikel anc: In the Annals of the Kaqchikels, the Obsidian Stone is the oracle at Tulan that sends the Kaqchikel ancestors out across the sea to find the hills and plains that will be their home.
the Prophet Muhammad: The Prophet Muhammad (about 570 to 632) is the founder of Islam. The saying is a hadith, a report of his words, recorded in the Sunan of Ibn Majah, one of the six canonical collections; it is quoted wherever Islamic learning is praised.
the Zoroastrian refugees, to the Rana of: The Qissa-i Sanjan, a Persian poem of about 1600, is the Parsi community's own account of how Zoroastrians fled Iran after the Arab conquest and were granted refuge on the coast of Gujarat by the local ruler, the Rana of Sanjan.
the children of the nobles of Israel, de: The Kebra Nagast, the Glory of Kings, is the Ethiopian national epic, set down in the fourteenth century. It tells how Menyelek, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, returned to Ethiopia with the firstborn sons of Israel's nobles, who lament the homes they leave.
the seafarer: The Seafarer is an Old English poem preserved in the tenth-century Exeter Book. Its speaker, who has known the hardships of the sea, feels the urge to set out again for the lands of strangers.
the wanderer: The Wanderer is an Old English poem preserved in the tenth-century Exeter Book. Its speaker is a warrior who has lost his lord and kin and must tread the paths of exile over the winter sea.
ʻŌlelo Noʻeau: ʻŌlelo noʻeau are Hawaiian proverbs and poetical sayings. Nearly three thousand were collected and explained by Mary Kawena Pukui, the great scholar of Hawaiian language and culture, in her 1983 anthology.
ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I (attr.): ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I (731 to 788) was an Umayyad prince who escaped the massacre of his family in Syria, crossed North Africa as a fugitive, and founded the emirate of Córdoba. The verses to a palm tree he planted are traditionally attributed to him.
Robert Burns: Robert Burns (1759 to 1796) is the national poet of Scotland. My Heart's in the Highlands, written in 1789 to an old air, was published in the Scots Musical Museum.
Robert Browning: Robert Browning (1812 to 1889) was an English poet who spent fifteen years living in Italy. Home-Thoughts, from Abroad, written there, is his best-known poem of longing for an English spring.
Xenophon, of the Ten Thousand sighting t: Xenophon (about 430 to 354 BCE) was an Athenian soldier and writer who helped lead ten thousand Greek mercenaries out of Persia after their employer's defeat in 401 BCE. His Anabasis records the moment the army, crossing the mountains, first saw the Black Sea and the way home.
the Herald, in Aeschylus: Aeschylus (about 525 to 456 BCE) was the first of the great Athenian tragedians. In his Agamemnon, produced in 458 BCE, a herald returning from the ten-year war at Troy greets the soil of Argos before the king himself arrives.
Tao Yuanming: Tao Yuanming (365 to 427) resigned his last official post after eighty days and went home to farm. His Return Home, written in 405, became the classic Chinese statement of leaving public life for one's own fields.
Ki no Tsurayuki, on the last night of th: Ki no Tsurayuki (about 872 to 945) was a Heian poet and the chief compiler of the Kokin Wakashū. His Tosa Diary records the sea voyage home to the capital after his term as governor of Tosa.
Abe no Nakamaro, in China, before the vo: Abe no Nakamaro (698 to 770) went to Tang China as a student at nineteen and rose high in the imperial service. His poem of homesickness is said to have been composed on the eve of a voyage home that shipwreck prevented; he died in China.
Kalidasa: Kalidasa was the greatest poet and dramatist of classical Sanskrit, active around the fifth century. The Cloud-Messenger is the lament of an exile who asks a passing monsoon cloud to carry a message to his wife.
Wang Wei: Wang Wei (699 to 759) was a Tang poet, painter and official, celebrated for short landscape poems. In this one a traveler from his home town is asked only whether the plum by the window has flowered.
Li Bai: Li Bai (701 to 762) is, with Du Fu, the most celebrated poet of the Tang dynasty, and traveled for most of his life. Quiet Night Thought is the poem every Chinese schoolchild learns first.
Catullus: Catullus (about 84 to 54 BCE) was a Roman lyric poet from Verona. His poem to Sirmio, the peninsula on Lake Garda where his family had a villa, was written on coming home from a year of service in Bithynia.
Odysseus, in Homer: Odysseus is the hero of Homer's Odyssey, who spends ten years after the fall of Troy trying to reach his home on Ithaca. He speaks these words at the court of the Phaeacians, refusing every offer of a better home elsewhere.
Rumi: Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207 to 1273) was a Persian poet and Sufi teacher. Born in Balkh, he was carried west as a child ahead of the Mongol invasions and settled in Konya; the opening of his Masnavi is the reed flute's lament for the reed bed it was cut from.
Dante Alighieri, in exile: Dante Alighieri (1265 to 1321) wrote the Divine Comedy in exile, having been banished from Florence in 1302 under sentence of death. In the Paradiso he imagines returning to be crowned as a poet at the font where he was baptised; he never did.
